title: Process Management
learning_outcomes: Describe Restart policies and explain how it relates to Process Management.
Demonstrate Process supervisors in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Container-managed processes.

content.intro: Process Management is part of deployment and production operations. This lesson connects Restart policies, Process supervisors, Container-managed processes to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: Production operations combine explicit configuration, repeatable builds, health signals, logging, graceful shutdown, and release discipline. Test a production-like start, configuration failure, health route, termination signal, and rollback procedure.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Production operations combine explicit configuration, repeatable builds, health signals, logging, graceful shutdown, and release discipline. Keep secrets in the deployment environment, provide health checks, and stop accepting new work before draining in-flight work.

Run with `node example.mjs` when the example is self-contained, or adapt the required imports/inputs first.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Process Management. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with Restart policies; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.
Test one failure or boundary case for Process supervisors, then explain why the outcome is expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a successful local run proves deployment, database access, external services, or shutdown behavior are correct.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Document deployment assumptions and verify them in a controlled environment before announcing readiness.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
